html:
In the 1700s the steppe nomads of Central Asia lost the military edge they had held for two thousand years. Their great neighbours, Qing China and Russia, closed in on them with forts, cannon and muskets.

For centuries mounted archers from the steppe could beat larger farming armies, as the Mongol Empire showed. The French historian Fernand Braudel argued that gunpowder changed this: speed no longer beat firepower, and cannon could hold a fort that horsemen could not take.

The squeeze began when Russia and China split the northern lands between them in the Treaty of Nerchinsk of 1689. The last great steppe empire, the Dzungar Khanate, was destroyed by the Qing in the 1750s. To the west, the Kazakhs came under Russian protection and lines of Russian forts. After this the nomads no longer threatened the empires; the empires ruled them.
